nameStory: Late figwort gets its name because it blooms later in the season than its cousin, common figwort. The 'figwort' part comes from an old belief that these plants could cure 'figs' - painful growths and swellings. One of its other names, 'carpenter's square,' refers to the distinctive square stems that look like the tool carpenters use to make right angles.
description: Late figwort is a tall, sturdy wildflower that can tower over you at 5-10 feet high, making it one of our tallest native wildflowers. It has a distinctive square stem and large, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs up the stem. The small, unusual flowers are clustered at the top and have a unique shape that some say looks like a tiny horse's mouth with an overbite. Despite its impressive height, many people walk right past this common but overlooked native plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny rounded flowers (about 1/3 inch) with a cup-like opening that resembles a horse's mouth with an overbite. Deep reddish-purple inside, greenish-brown outside, clustered in branching sprays at the top of the plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Impressively tall at 5-10 feet, with a sturdy, distinctly square stem that you can feel with your fingers. The plant stands upright and unbranched until the flowering top.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large oval leaves up to 6 inches long, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Feel slightly rough to the touch with visible veins and serrated (toothed) edges.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small brown capsules that split open to release tiny dark seeds. The dried seed clusters persist into winter, creating interesting architectural shapes.

habitat: Look for late figwort in dry to semi-dry woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout New England. It prefers partially shaded areas with well-drained soil and is often found along trails, in forest openings, or where the woods meet fields. You'll sometimes spot it growing near other tall woodland herbs in disturbed or semi-open areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground as thick, square stems. Large opposite leaves unfurl and the plant rapidly gains height through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full height by midsummer. Distinctive reddish-purple flowers bloom in late summer (July-September), attracting hummingbirds and small pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small brown seed capsules develop. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, but the square stems remain visible.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stems with empty seed capsules persist through winter, creating distinctive skeletal remains that help with identification.

funFact: Hummingbirds are frequent visitors to late figwort's tiny flowers in late summer, even though the blooms seem almost too small for these feisty birds - but the flowers are perfectly sized for the hummingbirds' needle-like beaks and provide an important late-season nectar source when many other flowers have finished blooming.
confusionNotes: The tall square stem and large opposite leaves might remind you of plants in the mint family, but late figwort's unusual horse-mouth flowers are completely different from mint's typical tube-shaped blooms. Remember: square stem plus weird flowers equals figwort, square stem plus minty smell equals mint family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its past medicinal uses for hemorrhoids and anxiety (hence old names like 'pilewort' and 'heal-all'), late figwort should never be used for home remedies. The plant contains compounds that can be harmful if consumed, so admire it for its ecological value and unique beauty instead.
compareHints: Late figwort blooms later than common figwort and grows taller, often reaching 8-10 feet versus common figwort's more modest 3-5 feet. Lanceleaf figwort, as its name suggests, has much narrower, lance-shaped leaves rather than the broad oval leaves of late figwort. The flowering time is your best clue - late figwort truly lives up to its name by blooming well into late summer.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common figwort can be distinguished from late figwort by its more northern range and slightly smaller flowers, while lanceleaf figwort has much narrower, lance-shaped leaves rather than the broad, oval leaves of common figwort.
Lanceleaf figwort differs from common figwort by having narrower, more lance-shaped leaves (rather than broadly oval ones) and generally growing taller and more slender.
